brief_extract:
(Courtesy of Highland News)

TRAVELLERS' TALES
THIS is the season for "armchair travel", and this issue of The Electrical Age contains some interesting travellers' tales. While the narratives transport readers on exciting mental journeys to the Soviet Union and to Western Germany where the varied backgrounds of these countries are so different from the familiar one of the United Kingdom, the travellers also indicate the factual information which they will be presenting in lectures at a later date. The visit to Russia was to study the employment of women engineers, and the tour in Western Germany was to study domestic electrification.

brief_context: River winding through the centre of Leningrad.
article_title: A STUDY TOUR OF THE USSR
brief_extract: The city was very badly damaged during the 1939-45 War but is now almost completely rebuilt, and so skilfully has the rebuilding been done—keeping the old 19th century design of architecture—that it is difficult to tell what is old and what is new. A delightful town with the River Neva winding through its centre. One's first impression of the town is one of broad unlittered streets, large open public squares, golden spires and domes, unsmiling and slightly drab people and colourful gardens.

brief_context: Palace visited just outside Leningrad.
article_title: A STUDY TOUR OF THE USSR
brief_extract: On Saturday morning the sun shone brightly and the air was clear and sparkling. Our guide suggested a visit to the Summer Palace of Peter just outside Leningrad, and there we spent an all-too-short hour strolling in the grounds—grounds made lovely by fantastic gilded fountains and blending with the golden and russet tints of autumn. Our visit had to be cut short for our flight south to Moscow.

brief_context: Where the Queen made remarks on education for women.
brief_extract: I only wish a photograph could have been taken of the Queen standing beside the electric cooker in the kitchen and discussing home affairs with the proud tenants. The Queen's deep devotion to her family life is well known, and her remarks on the education of women during a recent visit to Oxford were therefore of special interest. The Queen pointed out that a woman need not barter her intellectual life for the happiness and deep satisfaction of bringing up a family and that nowadays a woman could keep the one without endangering her chances of the other.

brief_context: Ancient Greek city known for its inhabitants' dislike of noise.
brief_extract:
CONFORMS TO BRITISH STANDARD 3456]

The Problem of Noise
As communities become more sophisticated so they become more sensitive to noise. At least that was the experience, according to tradition, of the affluent Greek city of Sybaris whose people disliked noise so much that they forbade not only the din of the smithy but the crowing of cocks. Certainly, in the stage of civilisation which we have reached, we seem to be increasingly conscious of noise.

brief_extract:
GOLDSMITHS' HALL
HISTORY OF THE HALL
THE Hall of the Worshipful Company of Goldsmiths is one of the few in the City of London which carries on the functions for which it was founded in mediaeval times. The hall is the fourth to stand on the site which was in the heart of the area where the mediaeval goldsmiths lived and worked.

location_standardised: Foster Lane, London, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Site of the first Goldsmiths' Hall built around 1340.
article_title: GOLDSMITHS' HALL: HISTORY OF THE HALL
brief_extract: The hall is the fourth to stand on the site which was in the heart of the area where the mediaeval goldsmiths lived and worked. The first hall in Fosters Lane was built about 1340. The second hall was probably begun about 1407 and included a chapel, armoury, granary and assay office.

brief_context: Origin of the tapestries depicting the life of St. Dunstan.
article_title: GOLDSMITHS' HALL: HISTORY OF THE HALL
brief_extract: The second hall was probably begun about 1407 and included a chapel, armoury, granary and assay office. The Tudor hall was very rich and hung with Flanders tapestries depicting the life of St. Dunstan, patron saint of goldsmiths.

brief_context: Place where St. Dunstan served as Archbishop and cast bells.
article_title: GOLDSMITHS' HALL: HISTORY OF THE HALL
brief_extract: Dunstan, patron saint of goldsmiths. A 10th century Archbishop of Canterbury, he was interested in crafts and himself cast bells for Canterbury. Inigo Jones was consulted about the third Hall, built in the 1630s, but damaged in the Great Fire of 1666.

brief_context: Mentioned as the ancient civilization that created papyrus.
article_title: PAPER IN THE HOME ... material of a thousand uses
brief_extract: The manufacture of paper is very old indeed. We know that the ancient Egyptians made it and, indeed, some of their papyrus (hence our word ‘paper’) has been preserved for us to see to this day. Its uses then and until late mediaeval times were entirely for the recording of knowledge and information by means of writing or pictorial illustration.

brief_context: Reference to the style of cut velvets imitated by wallpaper.
article_title: PAPER IN THE HOME ... material of a thousand uses
brief_extract:
They next found that it was possible to ‘repeat’ a design indefinitely, and so in the late fourteenth and fifteenth centuries papers made expressly for wall coverings began to make their appearance. Wallpaper
Right up to the middle of the nineteenth century wallpapers were used largely by the middle classes who were thus able to ape the wealthy in their choice of wall coverings — for paper could be printed to resemble tapestry hangings or be sprayed with flock to resemble rich Genoese cut velvets and brocades. Even wood was quite successfully imitated.

brief_context: Origin of expensive imported wallpaper mentioned as an eighteenth-century vogue.
article_title: PAPER IN THE HOME ... material of a thousand uses
brief_extract: Even wood was quite successfully imitated. However, apart from a vogue in the eighteenth century amongst the nobility for very expensive imported Chinese papers, the wallpaper trade continued without much excitement until the year of the Great Exhibition in 1851. Then the first machine-made (and therefore cheaper) wallpapers were shown to the general public.

AWARDS TO WOMEN

Second Scholarship at Cambridge University
The Caroline Haslett Memorial Trust has awarded a scholarship at Cambridge University to Miss Cynthia Shepherd of Chislehurst, Kent, who will read for the Natural Sciences Tripos at New Hall, and will specialise in physics, with a view to making her career in electrical engineering. In answering all these enquiries it has to be remembered that where there is a difference in the voltage of the supply in the new country it may be nearly as expensive to rewind the element of the appliance as to buy a new one.

brief_extract:
N. SHERBORNE, Committee Member, Woolwich

Woolwich members were the first women to be taken round the Belvedere Generating Station, although many parties of men from Great Britain and overseas visit the Station. The Station is being erected on land reclaimed from the Marshes, and the construction started in 1954.

brief_extract:
N. SHERBORNE, Committee Member, Woolwich

Woolwich members were the first women to be taken round the Belvedere Generating Station, although many parties of men from Great Britain and overseas visit the Station. The Station is being erected on land reclaimed from the Marshes, and the construction started in 1954.

brief_context: Location of refineries supplying oil to the station.
article_title: Special Events in E.A.W. Branches - VISIT TO BELVEDERE GENERATING STATION
brief_extract: The ultimate capacity will be 480,000 kW and will com-prise four 60,000 kW generators and two 120,000 kW generators. The Station burns low grade fuel oil which is delivered to the site by river tankers from refineries in the Thames Estuary, and 2,000 tons of oil will be burnt each day when the station is in full commission. Each set is supplied with steam from its own unit boiler.

brief_context: Rayners School was unique in Britain for such children.

brief_extract: The history of the school goes back to 1900. brief_context: Associated with the title of Lord Disraeli.

Household Management" observes that:

It is doubtful whether the feathered or furry
game of the British Isles now gratify a large
number of palates, because many people,
particularly of the younger generation, have
never tasted them. Game must be hung to allow
it to develop its characteristic flavours, and well
hung game (which is a polite way of saying that
the carcase is at some stage of decomposition)
does not fit into an age of food "untouched by
human hand", or that is reared hygienically in
batteries by the thousand.

A WEST COUNTRY farm is a delightful place for a summer holiday, but in the cold and wet of spring, autumn and winter the inescapable chores can be very unpleasant. Small wonder then that four West Country farmers recently gave the verdict that “On amenity grounds alone electricity is worth every penny that is paid”.

brief_context: Where the reports on farm electrification were published.
brief_extract: The South-Western Electricity Board carried out an investigation on these four farms to study the effect of electricity on farming, and the reports are published by the Board and by Bristol University’s Department of Agricultural Economics. They are the first reports of their kind published in Britain. The farms all have delightful names — Charmeydown, near Bath; Higher Monkton, Stogursey, Somerset; Crablake, Exminster, Devon; and Great Hewas, Truro, Cornwall.

brief_extract: D. SIMPSON, Chairman, Dunfermline. Members visited the Rehabilitation Centre of the Bridge of Earn Hospital, where most of the equipment was electrically operated.

brief_context: Origin of patients attending the rehabilitation centre.
article_title: VISIT TO REHABILITATION CENTRE, BRIDGE OF EARN HOSPITAL
brief_extract: Many of the very simple devices used at the centre have been thought out and fashioned on the premises by the patients during occupational therapy courses, and have been copied by medical visitors from overseas. Patients come from as far as the Shetland Islands and on occasions from the North of England and from Northern Ireland. Members were delighted to hear of successes such as this: a man crippled in all his limbs from birth was admitted at 26 years-of-age and within 15 months was discharged and found work with Remploy, formerly he could not dress or feed himself, and now he could attend to his own needs, had mastered a set of drums and was the "relief" in a ballroom orchestra.
